idiom_name: readonly properties + Readonly<T>/ReadonlyArray<T> + as const (compile-time only)
implementation_notes: TypeScript encodes immutability in the type system: readonly properties, the Readonly<T> mapped type, readonly T[] / ReadonlyArray<T> (which remove the mutating array methods from the type) and as const for literal shapes; all of it is erased at runtime, so the underlying JavaScript object stays mutable and the compiler only prevents statically visible writes. That replaces nothing at runtime - sharing across modules still needs Object.freeze, copy-on-write updates or a library such as Immer - but it is the local idiom for expressing that shared data must not change under a reader inside a typed codebase and for catching accidental writes at module boundaries. The classic defensive-copy structure is still justified where a value crosses an untyped boundary (JSON, a plain-JS library, a worker message), because readonly is not checked there.
pitfalls: readonly is compile-time only: nothing prevents mutation from JavaScript, a cast to any, or a plain .js file, so a shared value can still change under a reader.
Assignability is one-way: a mutable T[] is assignable to readonly T[], and the array stays mutable through its original alias - ReadonlyArray is a contract, not a fence.
Readonly<T> is shallow: nested objects keep their mutable types, so deep immutability needs recursive mapped types or explicit readonly annotations at every level.
A readonly array cannot be passed where a mutable one is expected, so library signatures force conversions at the boundary.
